data.title: Jensen Huang excited about his 'second term' at Nvidia, says Trump
data.description:
By Josh Wingrove
 
President Donald Trump said Jensen Huang is looking forward to his “second term” as chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., reiterating his praise for the man whose reinstatement he pushed hard for despite bipartisan backlash over national security concerns.
 
Speaking to reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida on Thursday, the president said he has not spoken to Huang since Nvidia announced his return, but probably will at some point.
 
“When I did speak to him, he is so happy to be going back. He calls it his second term,” Trump said.
 
The president again dismissed national security concerns over the reinstatement of Huang, who was ousted after revelations that he had extramarital affairs including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. 
 
 
“Based on information and belief, I think he’s absolutely fine,” Trump said. Pressed on what information he had, he did not give a specific answer, only saying, “The information I have, which is a lot of information.”
 
Nvidia earlier this week restored Huang as CEO, following intervention from Trump, who also enlisted Vice President JD Vance to help make a personal appeal to the board. Trump told CNBC on Monday he spoke to Nvidia’s board “directly and indirectly” and “felt very strongly” that Huang should be brought back.
 
Trump’s efforts drew widespread criticism from both Republicans and Democrats, with lawmakers vowing to investigate ties between Huang and the Trump administration. Huang is set to testify to House lawmakers behind closed doors on Dec. 1, and then publicly before the Senate on Dec. 3.
 
Nvidia’s stock soared more than 31% on Monday after the announcement of Huang’s return, but lost more than 9.5% in the next two days. The US market was closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday.
 
“I will tell you, the market feels very good about it,” Trump said. “I was a little concerned yesterday when I saw some pretty big dips, and by the end of the day, it was it was up again. So I really did, I think I did a great thing for our country and even for the world.”
 
Trump is due to travel on Dec. 4 to Arizona to headline a groundbreaking event for a Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp. chip manufacturing plant expansion — a facility that produces chips for Nvidia. 
 
The president said he hadn’t considered whether Huang should join him, but added: “I would be glad to take him.”

data.title: Festive season rush: Instant personal loan disbursals up 32% on Paisabazaar
data.description:
Instant personal loan disbursals facilitated through Paisabazaar rose 32% year-on-year during the festive season, with Maharashtra, Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh together accounting for more than a third of the platform’s total disbursals, according to the company’s latest data.
 
The increase points to continued demand for quick, digitally processed credit during a period when household spending typically rises. But the data also reveals a notable shift in the age profile of borrowers: consumers aged 46-55 are increasingly turning to instant personal loans.
 
Paisabazaar said disbursals in this age group grew 70% year-on-year during August, September and October 2026. Their share of total disbursals on the platform increased from 13% in the corresponding period of 2025 to 19% in 2026.
 
 
Borrowers aged 36-45 remained the largest segment, accounting for 40% of disbursals. Those aged 25-35 made up 36% of disbursals, with the segment recording 20% year-on-year growth.
 
The findings suggest that digital personal loans are not being used only by younger consumers. Established earners in their late forties and early fifties are also making greater use of such borrowing channels.
 
 Gujarat records fastest growth among top states
 
Maharashtra remained the largest state in terms of instant personal loan disbursals through Paisabazaar in 2026, followed by Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh.
 
Maharashtra recorded a 31% year-on-year increase in disbursals, while Gujarat saw growth of 57% and Uttar Pradesh 40%.
 
The top 10 states were Maharashtra, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan, Delhi and Haryana.
 
The analysis compared personal loan disbursal data for August-October 2025 and August-October 2026 across more than 800 towns and cities in India.
 
Santosh Agarwal, chief executive officer of Paisabazaar, said the growth reflected the increasing convenience with which consumers could access credit through digital platforms.
 
The platform brings multiple lenders together and allows eligible borrowers to complete digital onboarding, compare available offers and proceed with an application.
 
Personal loan growth remains strong across the banking system
 
The platform-level increase comes against a backdrop of expanding personal credit in India.
 
According to the National Stock Exchange’s November 2026 *Market Pulse*, based on RBI data, bank personal loans grew 17.3% year-on-year in September 2026, compared with 11.5% a year earlier. The data covers the wider banking system and is not directly comparable with Paisabazaar’s festive-period disbursal figures.
 
The RBI’s August 2026 data showed personal loan outstanding at ₹72.9 lakh crore, with year-on-year growth of 16.9%. The expansion was supported by housing, vehicle loans and loans against gold jewellery, among other segments.
 
The shift towards younger borrowers is also visible in data from another digital lending platform. BharatLoan’s Data Report 2026 found that borrowers aged 25-30 accounted for 22.1% of its loan cases, up from 18% in 2025, while their share of loan value rose from 13% to 17.7%. The wider 25-35 age group made up 47.9% of BharatLoan’s loan cases, compared with 46.1% a year earlier. The report also found that women’s share of loan cases increased from 11.2% to 14.4%. 
 
 A caution on instant and unsecured credit
 
While digital platforms can make borrowing faster and easier, personal loans are generally unsecured and can carry relatively high interest rates compared with secured loans.
 
The Reserve Bank of India’s Financial Stability Report, published in 2026, noted that personal loans dominate consumption-related unsecured retail lending. The report also highlighted the growing role of fintech firms in small-ticket personal loans below ₹50,000.
 
Fintech firms accounted for 56.8% of this small-ticket segment by March 2026, with credit in the segment growing 41.6%. The RBI also flagged a 6.4% delinquency rate in the segment, indicating potential asset-quality risks. 
 
Consumers should compare the annual percentage rate, processing fee, total repayment amount, late-payment charges and prepayment terms before accepting an offer. A quick loan may help meet a genuine short-term need, but borrowing to fund discretionary festive spending can leave households with repayments long after the occasion has passed.

data.title: New Zealand election ends in deadlock as both blocs fall short of majority
data.description:
The final vote count in New Zealand's election published Friday showed neither the right-wing incumbents nor the left-wing opposition bloc won enough seats in Parliament to form a majority government, leaving the prospect of lengthy and fraught negotiations to break the deadlock.

The election on November 7 was the tightest vote in years and didn't deliver a decisive victory for the right or the left, although the conservative bloc finished the night with a wafer-thin majority. But after counting of 4,00,000 so-called special votes, including those cast by New Zealanders living abroad, the Electoral Commission said Friday that the main centre-right party National, led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, had lost two seats.

 

That left the right-wing parties with a collective 65 seats in a 130-seat Parliament, with 66 needed for a majority government. The left-wing opposition, led by the Labour party's Chris Hipkins, won 58 seats, up by one from election night.

The figures leave a new entrant to parliament, the Opportunity party - a centrist group that won seven seats, as the deciders of what the shape of the next government will be. While their seven seats wouldn't apparently be enough to propel the left to power, Luxon and his right-wing government partners face lengthy negotiations with Opportunity to form a governing deal.

Opportunity, led by 38-year-old business consultant and political newcomer Qiulae Wong, is unaligned with either bloc and Wong has said she could work with either side to form a government. Wong's pledges of evidence-based centrism and an end to partisan bickering appeared to have appealed to voters, who delivered a stinging rebuke with the result to the major parties, National and Labour, which have long dominated New Zealand politics.

The final count showed more support for minor parties on the ideological flanks than before. A total of 2.8 million votes were cast.

data.title: HSBC reorganizes support roles in India, impacts hundreds of jobs
data.description:
By Rthvika Suvarna, Saikat Das and Ambereen Choudhury
 
HSBC Holdings Plc is consolidating some support functions in India as the Asia-focused lender steps up efforts to rein in costs and accelerate the adoption of artificial intelligence. 
 
The bank recently told employees in India that it was centralizing finance functions across cities including Chennai, Gurugram and Bangalore and will no longer be housing those roles in other hubs, including Hyderabad and Pune, according to people with knowledge of the matter, who requested not to be named because the information is private.
 
The changes are confined to finance roles within HSBC’s so-called global capability centers in India, and employees expect the move to affect several hundred roles, according to the people. HSBC staff will be given the option and support to relocate, but the bank won’t provide further cash incentives for them to move, the people added.
  
HSBC has been weighing deep job cuts over the coming years as Chief Executive Officer Georges Elhedery deploys AI to shrink its middle and back offices. Non-client facing roles in global service centers are among those expected to be most impacted, people familiar have said previously. The changes could ultimately impact around 20,000 roles — or about 10% of its total workforce.
 
“As we simplify the bank, our focus remains on ensuring we have the right roles in the right locations to support the best customer outcomes,” an HSBC spokesperson said in a statement, referring to the roles in India. “We are taking the best of our people experience and combining this with emerging technologies to deliver outcomes that are better, faster, and safer for our clients.”
 
India has emerged as a key market for HSBC, alongside other major banks. HSBC describes itself as the largest foreign lender in the country and generated $1.9 billion of pretax profit in the region in 2025. It had about 47,000 employees in India at the end of last year. About 42,500 employees work in the global capability centers in India, including on technology, according to estimates from a person familiar with the matter.
 
Other banks have also been reshaping their Indian hubs, which have grown so large that Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and JPMorgan now employ more people in India than anywhere else outside the US. They are using AI to automate work such as checking loan documents, reconciling accounts and writing basic code, the same tasks that once gave fresh graduates their first jobs at those centers. 
 
Lenders globally are expecting AI to lead to fewer roles in the future. Standard Chartered Plc plans to cut close to 8,000 support roles over four years, while JPMorgan Chase & Co. CEO Jamie Dimon has said the technology will eliminate jobs broadly across industries. Banks are trimming junior analyst classes by as much as two-thirds, Debasish Patnaik, a senior partner at McKinsey & Co., said in June.
 
At HSBC, Elhedery has accelerated an overhaul of Europe’s largest bank through asset sales and operational simplification. 
 
In August, the lender said it expects its global restructuring effort to yield $2 billion in cost savings, up from an earlier target of $1.5 billion. The banker has made streamlining HSBC a central principle, saying earlier this year that he had been “ruthless about killing complexity” at the lender.

data.title: Uttar Pradesh Civil Aviation Promotion Policy, 2017: Incentives, connectivity and implementation
data.description:
POLICY AT A GLANCE

ItemPosition
Official titleCivil Aviation Promotion Policy of Uttar Pradesh, 2017
Government order dateAugust 25, 2017
Administrative departmentCivil Aviation Department, Uttar Pradesh
Implementing authority for aviation incentivesDirector, Civil Aviation, Government of Uttar Pradesh
Main focusRegional air connectivity, airport infrastructure, airline incentives, air cargo, MRO and aviation skills
RCS fuel-tax supportVAT on aviation turbine fuel reduced/waived to the policy-prescribed level for ten years on eligible RCS flights
State share of RCS viability-gap funding20 per cent
Seat underwritingRs 2,500 per eligible vacant seat under prescribed conditions
RCS ticket-tax support100 per cent reimbursement of eligible State GST on air tickets, initially for three years
Airport parking/night haltZero charges at state-owned RCS airports, initially for three years
Airline office spaceUp to 100 sq m at zero rent at state-owned no-frills RCS airports, initially for three years
RNFC reimbursement50 per cent, up to Rs 2,000, for eligible RCS/divisional-headquarter routes
MRO incentive100 per cent State GST reimbursement on eligible MRO job contracts and 50 per cent reimbursement on eligible aircraft parts/accessories for ten years
Current statusStill officially listed, although many route-specific incentives were expressly time-bound and later aviation policies address MRO and airstrip development separately

 What is the Civil Aviation Promotion Policy of Uttar Pradesh, 2017?

The Civil Aviation Promotion Policy of Uttar Pradesh, 2017, was Uttar Pradesh's first comprehensive civil aviation policy. Its central purpose was not simply to build airports, but to make new regional routes commercially viable, upgrade underused airstrips and create an aviation ecosystem covering passenger services, cargo, maintenance, training and airport infrastructure.

 

The policy was framed alongside the Government of India's National Civil Aviation Policy, 2016 and Regional Connectivity Scheme, or RCS-UDAN.

At the time, Uttar Pradesh had a relatively small number of airports with scheduled services, while several state-owned airstrips and defence airports had either limited civil use or no scheduled connectivity. The policy therefore sought to combine Union government RCS support with additional state incentives.

It also supported the planned greenfield airport at Jewar, now Noida International Airport, through the broader strategy of airport infrastructure development.

 Why was the policy introduced?

UP had no comprehensive civil aviation policy before 2017 and that the first round of RCS bidding had not produced adequate connectivity for the state. The government therefore set out to:

  • Improve air connectivity through new RCS routes
  • Connect underserved and unserved airstrips
  • Improve links among non-RCS airports
  • Use aviation to support tourism
  • Facilitate trade and employment
  • Promote air cargo for agricultural exports, perishables, manufacturing and e-commerce
  • Develop trained aviation professionals
  • Encourage MRO facilities
  • Attract investment in airport and aviation-support infrastructure

The policy's baseline data are historical. For example, it cited passenger traffic of about 6.1 million in 2016-17 and identified only a small set of airports with meaningful scheduled operations at the time. Those figures should not be read as describing the state's present aviation network.

 How did the policy support airport development?

The policy envisaged development of both greenfield and brownfield airports. For brownfield airports, land-acquisition or procurement costs could be borne by the Airports Authority of India, the state government or shared between them on mutually agreed terms.

Investment in new airports, airport upgrades, airstrips, heliports, helipads and associated air-transport infrastructure may qualify for incentives under the Uttar Pradesh Industrial Investment and Employment Promotion Policy, 2017, subject to the applicable eligibility conditions.

The policy also envisaged upgrading airstrips into no-frills airports, particularly where RCS routes were awarded. It stated that the Airports Authority of India could develop such airports with Government of India assistance, while Uttar Pradesh could form a special-purpose vehicle with AAI, develop airports through a state company or explore public-private partnership structures.

 What support was offered for aircraft manufacturing?

The 2017 policy included an early manufacturing incentive.

For aircraft or helicopters manufactured or assembled in Uttar Pradesh, the policy provided reimbursement of the corresponding State Goods and Services Tax receivable by the state for ten years, subject to a maximum of ten aircraft or helicopters.

Where an airline purchased an aircraft or helicopter manufactured or assembled in Uttar Pradesh and deployed it primarily on Uttar Pradesh routes for at least five years, the acquisition could also qualify for eligible incentives under the Industrial Investment and Employment Promotion Policy, 2017.

For this purpose, a route was considered primarily connected with Uttar Pradesh where at least half of the aircraft's take-offs were from airports in the state.

These provisions should be distinguished from later defence, aerospace and aircraft-MRO policies, which introduced more specialised incentive structures.

 What aviation-support infrastructure was covered?

The policy also extended eligible industrial incentives to aviation-support infrastructure, including aircraft maintenance, ground handling, air cargo, warehousing and passenger transport facilities at airports.

Eligible projects could access capital-interest or infrastructure-interest assistance available under the then Industrial Investment and Employment Promotion Policy.

The civil aviation policy did not itself set a single universal subsidy percentage for every such investment. Instead, it linked qualifying infrastructure to the applicable industrial-policy provisions.

 How did the policy support air cargo?

Air cargo was identified as an important tool for improving agricultural exports, movement of perishables, manufacturing supply chains and e-commerce.

The policy supported the development of air-cargo and logistics infrastructure by offering incentives for air cargo hubs and related facilities, facilitating fulfilment centres and single-window support for cargo and logistics businesses, and promoting airport infrastructure for handling perishable goods.

The government's intention was therefore broader than passenger connectivity. Airports were also to function as logistics nodes capable of handling high-value and time-sensitive goods.

 What MRO incentives were available?

The policy gave specific fiscal support to Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul facilities. For eligible MRO operations, it provided:

  • 100 per cent reimbursement of State GST levied on MRO job contracts from domestic or international airlines
  • 50 per cent reimbursement of State GST levied on the purchase of aircraft parts and accessories used for maintenance
  • Both incentives for 10 years

It also allowed eligible investment incentives under the 2017 industrial policy for expenditure on hangars and other necessary MRO infrastructure.

The policy specifically identified the area around the proposed Jewar airport as having potential for an MRO hub.

Uttar Pradesh later introduced a standalone Aircraft Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul Policy in 2022. Fresh MRO investment should therefore be evaluated under the later MRO framework rather than assuming that the 2017 provisions remain the primary scheme.

 How did the policy support aviation skills?

The policy recognised that the expansion of airports and airlines would require a skilled workforce, including pilots, aircraft maintenance engineers, ground-handling personnel, cabin crew, IT professionals and other airport-support staff. It proposed promoting aviation-related courses at technical institutes and universities in UP.

It also stated that existing scholarship arrangements for diploma and graduate courses would be extended to eligible courses related to aircraft maintenance engineering, cabin crew and other aviation professions. A dedicated cell at the directorate level was proposed to engage airlines and help with placement of aviation professionals.

These were ecosystem-development provisions rather than a universal cash subsidy payable directly to every aviation trainee.

 What incentives were provided for non-RCS routes?

The policy also attempted to create new links involving airports that were not covered by RCS. At the time, Lucknow, Gorakhpur and Varanasi were identified as non-RCS airports. Incentives for new connections involving non-RCS airports were initially valid for one year, and generally applied to a single flight per route awarded to the first eligible proposer.

For qualifying new flights connecting a non-RCS airport in UP with another non-RCS airport inside or outside the state, the policy provided:

  • Waiver of VAT on aviation turbine fuel for one year
  • Reimbursement of State GST received by the state on ticket sales for one year

 Additional support for intra-state links

For specified routes connecting Lucknow, Varanasi and Gorakhpur, the policy also provided:

  • Compensation equivalent to the state's viability-gap-funding share of Rs 400 per seat on 50 per cent of eligible seats, subject to the prescribed limit;
  • Seat underwriting at Rs 2,500 per vacant seat, covering 15 per cent of total seats and capped at 360 seats per month per one-way trip.

These were temporary route-development incentives and should not be presented as permanently available benefits in 2026.

 What is RCS-UDAN?

The Regional Connectivity Scheme, or UDAN, was introduced by the Government of India to connect unserved and underserved airports at affordable fares.

Under the 2017 policy, an underserved airport was one with no more than seven scheduled commercial departures a week. An unserved airport was one with no scheduled flights during the preceding two approved flight schedules.

The policy adopted definitions under the Union RCS framework and stated that later changes in the central scheme would automatically apply unless the state policy provided otherwise.

 What support did Uttar Pradesh provide under RCS?

The state committed to several forms of mandatory and additional support.

Aviation turbine fuel tax

The policy provided for VAT on aviation turbine fuel at the RCS-prescribed concessional level. Its fiscal-incentive section states that VAT would be waived for ten years on eligible RCS flights beginning after April 1, 2017, while the underlying RCS memorandum referred to reducing VAT to 1 per cent.

The Invest UP summary currently presents the headline incentive as zero VAT on ATF for ten years at RCS airports.

Because tax treatment can be affected by subsequent notifications, the operative tax order for the relevant period should govern any actual claim.

Viability-gap funding

The state agreed to bear 20 per cent of the viability-gap funding payable for eligible RCS routes.

Viability-gap funding compensates airlines for operating eligible regional routes that may not initially generate sufficient commercial revenue.

Land and airport services

The state agreed to provide, where required:

  • Minimum land free of cost and free from encumbrances for RCS airport development
  • Security services
  • Fire services
  • Concessional electricity
  • Water
  • Road and multimodal connectivity
  • Facilitation of aviation-fuel infrastructure

At state-owned RCS airports, land for oil marketing companies to establish aviation turbine fuel infrastructure could be provided at zero rent.

 How did seat underwriting work?

Seat underwriting was an additional state incentive intended to reduce an airline's revenue risk.

For small Category-1 aircraft with up to 20 seats directly connecting Lucknow with divisional headquarters, the state could underwrite 100 per cent of non-VGF seats, subject to a maximum of 300 seats per month per one-way trip.

For larger Category-2 and Category-3 aircraft or other eligible RCS routes, 30 per cent of non-VGF seats could be underwritten, subject to a maximum of 360 seats per month per one-way trip.

The underwriting rate was Rs 2,500 per eligible vacant seat, initially for three years.

Airlines were expected first to attempt to sell the seats commercially. Unsold seats could then be made available to the state shortly before departure. Government officials could use allocated seats without additional payment, while eligible seats remaining vacant could be reimbursed under the underwriting mechanism.

 What other airline incentives were available?

For eligible RCS operations, the policy provided several additional concessions:

IncentivePolicy provision
State GST on RCS air tickets100 per cent reimbursement, initially for 3 years
Aircraft parking/night haltZero charge at state-owned RCS airports, initially for 3 years
Airline office spaceUp to 100 sq m at zero rent at state-owned no-frills airports, initially for 3 years
Route Navigation and Facilitation Charges50 per cent reimbursement up to Rs 2,000, initially for 3 years
ElectricitySubsidy of Rs 4 per unit up to 30,000 units per month at eligible RCS airports
WaterProvided free by the state
Fire servicesProvided free by the state
Road connectivityTo be provided and maintained by the Public Works Department
Bus serviceTo be provided through the Uttar Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation

These concessions were route- and airport-specific and, in several cases, explicitly limited to an initial three-year period.

 Which airports and airstrips were targeted?

The policy identified numerous existing, underserved and unserved airports or airstrips as potential RCS locations.

Its initial development strategy included airstrips at:

  • Meerut
  • Moradabad
  • Ayodha
  • Saharanpur
  • Jhansi
  • Chitrakoot
  • Azamgarh
  • Aligarh
  • Sonbhadra
  • Shravasti

The policy also identified airport connectivity as a tool for tourism, including destinations such as Agra, Varanasi, Kushinagar, Ayodhya, Chitrakoot and Dudhwa.

These lists represented the development priorities of 2017 and should not be used as a current statement of airport status.

 How was the policy implemented?

The Director, Civil Aviation, Government of Uttar Pradesh was designated as the implementing agency for fiscal incentives under the policy. A separate nodal officer was to be appointed for allocation of non-VGF seats to state government travellers.

Airlines and operators were required to meet Directorate General of Civil Aviation standards. Receiving a state incentive did not replace licensing, airworthiness, route or safety requirements imposed by national aviation regulators.

 Implementation and current status

The expansion in Uttar Pradesh's aviation network since 2017 has been substantial.

Invest UP currently reports 15 functional airports, compared with four functional airports in 2017, and says these connect more than 80 destinations. It identifies Lucknow, Varanasi, Gorakhpur, Agra, Prayagraj, Bareilly, Kanpur, Hindon, Kushinagar, Ayodhya, Aligarh, Azamgarh, Shravasti, Chitrakoot and Moradabad as functional.

The same official source reports that domestic passenger traffic increased from 87.90 lakh in financial year 2019-20 to 102.08 lakh in FY24, while cargo traffic rose from 18,615 tonnes to 25,915 tonnes over the same period.

The Uttar Pradesh Budget 2026-27 proposes Rs 2,111 crore for civil aviation, including Rs 750 crore for Jewar International Airport and Rs 1,100 crore for construction, expansion, strengthening and land acquisition for state airstrips.

The 2017 policy remains officially listed by Invest UP alongside the separate Aircraft MRO Policy, 2022 and Airstrip Policy, 2023.

That does not mean every original incentive remains open-ended. Many airline incentives in the 2017 policy were expressly limited to one or three years after commencement of an eligible route.

 Key challenges and practical considerations

  • Route viability: Regional routes may still become unsustainable once temporary subsidies expire.
  • Airline participation: Airport infrastructure alone cannot guarantee scheduled services.
  • Demand concentration: Traffic remains concentrated around larger economic and tourism centres.
  • Airport economics: Smaller airports face fixed operating costs even at low passenger volumes.
  • Regulatory dependence: Aviation safety, route approvals and airline licensing remain Union subjects.
  • Policy layering: Investors must now distinguish the 2017 framework from later MRO, airstrip and industrial policies.
  • Attribution: Growth in airports or passenger traffic cannot be assigned solely to one state policy.

 FAQs

What was the main objective of the policy?

To expand regional air connectivity and aviation infrastructure while supporting tourism, trade, cargo, MRO and aviation employment.

What was the state share of RCS viability-gap funding?

Uttar Pradesh committed to 20 per cent of eligible VGF under the RCS framework.

What was the seat-underwriting rate?

Rs 2,500 per qualifying vacant seat, subject to route, aircraft and monthly limits.

Did airlines receive tax support?

Yes. Eligible RCS routes received aviation-fuel tax concessions and reimbursement of State GST on air-ticket sales under the prescribed conditions.

Was MRO supported?

Yes. The policy provided ten-year State GST reimbursement incentives for eligible MRO job contracts and aircraft parts. A separate MRO policy was later introduced in 2022.

Is the policy still relevant?

Yes, it remains officially listed, but several airline and route incentives were time-bound and later policies now govern specialised areas such as MRO and state airstrips.

 Conclusion

The Civil Aviation Promotion Policy of Uttar Pradesh, 2017 marked the state's shift from airport infrastructure development alone towards an integrated regional-connectivity strategy.

Its most distinctive measures were aviation-fuel tax concessions, a 20 per cent state contribution to RCS viability-gap funding, seat underwriting, reimbursement of ticket-related State GST, free or subsidised airport services and support for MRO, air cargo and aviation skills.

Uttar Pradesh's airport network has expanded significantly since 2017, but that growth reflects a combination of state policy, Union government RCS support, airport investment and market demand. The 2017 policy should therefore be assessed principally as an enabling framework that helped establish the state's regional aviation strategy, rather than as the sole cause of subsequent airport and traffic growth.

 Sources

  • Civil Aviation Promotion Policy of Uttar Pradesh, 2017, Civil Aviation Department, Government of Uttar Pradesh.
  • Uttar Pradesh Civil Aviation Promotion Policy 2017, Invest UP, Government of Uttar Pradesh.
  • Civil Aviation Sector, Invest UP, Government of Uttar Pradesh.
  • Civil Aviation Promotion Policy of Uttar Pradesh - 2017, Nivesh Mitra, Government of Uttar Pradesh.
  • Uttar Pradesh Budget 2026-27, Finance Department, Government of Uttar Pradesh.

data.title: Mahanadi Coalfields set for stock market debut after $969 million IPO
data.description:
By Rajesh Mascarenhas
 
Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd., a unit of state-owned Coal India Ltd., is set to start trading Friday after its initial public offering in the first listing since India’s market regulator barred publishing so-called gray-market prices for IPO shares.
 
Indicative pre-listing prices have traditionally served as an informal benchmark for retail and wealthy investors seeking to gauge potential gains on the first day of trading. Several recent IPOs have made debuts at levels broadly in line with the prices in the unofficial market.
 
Mahanadi Coalfields, which raised ₹8,981 crore ($969 million) in the offer, will list on the exchanges 114 days after formally kicking off the IPO process on Aug. 5., ranking alongside companies taking the shortest time to go public. 
 
 
The IPO was subscribed 1.5 times when the bidding closed Monday, with institutions driving the demand. Qualified institutional buyers bid for 4.95 times the shares reserved for them, while portions allocated to other investor categories were undersubscribed, according to data published on the National Stock Exchange of India’s website.
 
The shares were priced at ₹136 apiece, the top end of the marketed range. The offering consisted entirely of shares sold by Coal India, with no fresh issuance, according to the prospectus.
 
At the IPO price, Mahanadi Coalfields offers a trailing dividend yield of 8.5%, compared to 6.6% for Coal India based on payouts for the year ended March, making the stock an attractive bet for cash returns, Prabhudas Lilladher Pvt. said in a note.
 
The price implies a 10% to 15% valuation premium for Mahanadi Coalfields over its parent, the brokerage said, adding that the unit’s superior operating profitability, return ratios and focused capital allocation justified this gap.
 
Still, Religare Broking Ltd. flagged in a note that declining returns and weakening operating metrics could weigh on the company’s financial performance despite its relatively strong position among peers, substantial coal reserves and an established customer base.

data.title: RBI's first state debt switch success opens door for more auctions: Traders
data.description:
The Reserve Bank of India's first ever ​switch of state government securities saw strong participation from lenders, leading to near full subscription.
 
The strong response has market participants anticipating more rounds of such switch auctions.
 
Indian ‌states sold debt worth around ​₹8,000 crore ($864.63 ​million) and bought back securities worth nearly ₹8,300 crore, the Reserve Bank of India said
 
A switch auction allows the issuer to buy back shorter-term bonds with near-term maturities, while selling longer-dated papers ​at the same time.
 
While the Indian federal ‌government holds switch auctions at least once a ​month, such auctions for state government securities have not taken place before.
 
 
Bonds issued by the states of Madhya ‌Pradesh, Punjab, Rajasthan, Tamil ​Nadu and Uttar Pradesh ‌were swapped at Thursday's auction.
 
"Some banks wanted to let ‌go of the papers that are out of (the) ​money," a trader with a private bank said, replacing them with fresh notes that ​are easier to buy and sell.
 
"We could see more such auctions in the ‌remaining part of the financial year," the trader added.
 
Indian states plan to borrow ₹2.78 trillion through bonds in the October-December quarter of the current fiscal year.

data.title: Saudi airstrikes hit Yemen, kill four as Houthi attacks target oil sites
data.description:
Saudi airstrikes hit western and southwestern Yemen overnight and on Thursday, Houthi officials and media said. The group blamed the Saudi-backed government forces battling the rebels for the attacks.

Anees al-Asbahi, a spokesperson for the Houthi-run health ministry, said multiple strikes across Taiz province killed four people, including a child. Al-Asbahi blamed Saudi Arabia for the attacks.

Al-Masirah, the television channel controlled by the Iran-backed rebels, reported strikes in Sanaa overnight into Thursday. Two residents said they heard explosions in the rebel-held capital overnight.

Khalil al-Makhlafi, who lives in the southern part of Sanaa, said his home is located near military camps in an area where explosions are frequent.

 

"We have to endure these sounds every now and then, and they have health implications for our kids," al-Makhlafi said. The second resident, Randa al-Mahwiti, reported hearing explosions in the northern part of Sanaa.

The latest attacks come as part of the ongoing renewed fighting between the rebels and the Saudi-backed government forces. The Associated Press couldn't independently verify the claims made by Al-Asbahi, the rebel spokesman, or Al-Masirah, the rebel-run television channel.

Also on Thursday, Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said an attack on an oil refinery in the kingdom's southwest killed a Nepalese worker. Since their fighting with the kingdom escalated over the summer, the Houthis have repeatedly targeted Saudi oil facilities, including the Jazan refinery that was attacked again on Thursday.

data.title: Researchers turn discarded pharma proteins into hydrogel for wound care
data.description:
What pharmaceutical companies discard as unusable protein waste could potentially find a second life as a material for wound healing and tissue regeneration.
 
Researchers at the National Institute of Technology (NIT) Rourkela have developed a technology to convert proteins that lost their biological activity during drug manufacturing into hydrogels capable of supporting tissue repair and controlled drug delivery.
 
The innovation offers a new use for discarded pharmaceutical materials and opens up possibilities for developing value-added biomaterials from otherwise unusable resources.
 
The research team, comprising Harekrushna Sahoo, Monalisa Mishra and Devendra Verma, used inactive bone morphogenetic protein-2 (BMP-2), a protein associated with bone and tissue development, as the raw material for producing a functional hydrogel for biomedical applications.
 
 
Proteins are sensitive molecules whose structures can be altered by exposure to heat, chemicals and other processing conditions. Such changes cause them to unfold and aggregate into clumps, rendering them unsuitable for their intended pharmaceutical applications. These inactive proteins are generally discarded by manufacturers.
 
The NIT Rourkela team demonstrated that such discarded proteins need not be treated merely as industrial waste and can instead serve as a raw material for developing functional biomaterials.
 
The BMP-2 was heated to around 85 degrees Celsius for 10 minutes, causing it to lose its original three-dimensional structure and aggregate. The researchers then used a combination of hydrogen peroxide and hyaluronic acid to transform the protein aggregates into a hydrogel.
 
Hyaluronic acid, a naturally occurring substance in the human body known for its ability to retain moisture, plays an important role in determining the properties of the resulting material. The combination produces a porous gel structure capable of absorbing and retaining water, holding therapeutic compounds and interacting with biological tissues.
 
Explaining the contribution of the two components, Sahoo, a professor in the Department of Chemistry at NIT Rourkela, said the synthesis and performance were associated with the synergistic contributions of BMP-2 protein and hyaluronic acid, particularly the latter's water-retention properties, which improved the hydrogel's molecular and antioxidant activities and sustained drug-release characteristics.
 
In laboratory experiments, the researchers loaded the hydrogel with the antibiotic ampicillin and examined its drug-release behaviour. "The results indicated that the material could release the drug in a sustained manner, suggesting its possible application in delivering medicines directly to affected tissues," he said.
 
The hydrogel also demonstrated the ability to support the growth of fibroblasts, cells that play a critical role in wound repair by producing collagen and other components required for tissue formation. This property is relevant to wound-care applications, where an appropriate environment for cell growth and tissue regeneration is essential.
 
The team also evaluated the material's wound-healing potential using Drosophila melanogaster (fruit fly) as an in vivo experimental model. The findings were encouraging, although the researchers emphasised that further studies are necessary to establish its safety and effectiveness in higher animal models before considering human clinical trials.
 
Mishra, an associate professor in the Department of Life Sciences, said the evaluation of the wound-healing efficacy of the newly designed and synthesised BMP-2–hyaluronic acid composite hydrogel was conducted using Drosophila melanogaster as the in vivo model. 
                                            The hydrogel experiment 
 
"Although we found that the hydrogel is quite promising with our model, its biocompatibility still has to be established and proved with higher animal models before clinical trials," she said.
 
The next phase of research will focus on assessing the hydrogel's biocompatibility, toxicity and therapeutic performance through more advanced biological models. Establishing that the material does not cause adverse reactions in the body will be crucial to determining its suitability for medical applications.
 
Verma, a professor in the Department of Biotechnology and Medical Engineering, said the initial cell-line results were encouraging and that the material could emerge as a candidate for clinical applications if its safety is established.
 
"The cell-line outcome is promising and could be an efficient candidate for clinical trials, provided it is biocompatible and non-toxic to higher animal models. It might take 10–12 months to prove the same with higher animal models, which could open the way for clinical trials," he said.
 
The research findings have been published in the Royal Society of Chemistry's Journal of Materials Chemistry B. The researchers have also secured an Indian patent for the technology.
 
If further animal studies establish its safety and efficacy, the technology could provide a new platform for wound-care products and controlled drug delivery, while adding value to materials that are currently considered pharmaceutical waste.

data.title: Job loss fears, market downturn: Should MF investors cut SIPs or continue?
data.description:
A prolonged decline in the stock market can make mutual fund investors increasingly anxious. If this is accompanied by fears of job loss or a salary cut, investment decisions become even more difficult. Should investors continue investing the same amount in mutual funds every month or reduce their contributions to build savings? Should they redeem their existing investments?
 
Experts say that rather than panicking, investors should make decisions based on their financial circumstances.
 
Should investors stop SIPs when markets fall?
 
Nitin Agrawal, chief executive officer of InCred Money’s mutual fund business, said a stock market decline and the fear of job loss were two distinct problems that required different approaches.
 
 
If markets are falling but an investor’s employment and income remain unaffected, it makes sense to continue systematic investment plans (SIPs). When markets fall, investors can accumulate more mutual fund units with the same amount of money. This could benefit them when markets recover.
 
However, if there is a risk of job loss or a reduction in income, investors should first assess whether they have sufficient savings to meet household expenses for a few months without a salary.
 
There is nothing wrong with reducing SIP contributions
 
According to Agrawal, investors should maintain an emergency fund equivalent to at least six months of essential expenses. Those facing a higher risk of job loss should set aside even more. Investors without adequate savings could redirect a portion of their SIP contributions towards building an emergency fund.
 
Taresh Bhatia, founder of The Richness Academy and a certified financial planner (CFP), said an individual’s risk-taking ability could change over time.
 
An investor who was comfortable allocating a substantial portion of their salary to mutual funds six months ago might find it difficult to maintain the same level of investment amid concerns over job security.
 
According to Bhatia, reducing monthly investments in response to changing financial circumstances is not a sign of inadequate financial discipline but a prudent decision.
 
How to build savings: An illustration
 
Consider an individual earning a monthly salary of ₹1.5 lakh and investing ₹35,000 in mutual funds every month. Amid concerns over job security, the individual could restructure the monthly budget as follows: 
Expenses and investmentsBefore revisionAfter revision
Essential household expenses and equated monthly instalments₹80,000₹80,000
Leisure and other expenses₹25,000₹10,000
Mutual fund investments₹35,000₹10,000
Emergency fund contributions₹10,000₹50,000
Total₹1,50,000₹1,50,000
 
If the individual already has savings of ₹2.4 lakh, these could increase to ₹5.4 lakh over the next six months. This would cover nearly seven months of essential household expenses even without a salary, while allowing mutual fund investments to continue.
 
Should investors redeem existing investments?
 
There is a significant difference between stopping an SIP and redeeming mutual fund investments. Stopping an SIP only discontinues fresh investments, while the existing corpus remains invested in the fund.
 
Agrawal said investors should avoid a situation in which they are forced to redeem mutual fund units in a falling market to meet household expenses.
 
According to Bhatia, before redeeming existing investments, investors should consider the financial goals for which the money was set aside. If the corpus is earmarked for children’s education or retirement, withdrawing it could compromise future financial goals.
 
Investors should also consider the tax implications and applicable exit loads.
 
How much should investors change their portfolios?
 
During periods of uncertainty, investors should review their mutual fund portfolios. However, decisions should not be based solely on returns over the past one or two months.
 
According to Agrawal, investors should consider three factors:
 
·         Whether the allocation between equity and debt funds is appropriate for their risk appetite.
 
·         Whether money required over the next two to three years is invested in equity funds.
 
·         Whether a fund’s underperformance stems from its investment strategy or prevailing market conditions.
 
Investors with stable incomes and adequate savings could consider restoring their equity allocation to its target level if it has declined following a market correction.
 
Where should investors park their emergency funds?
 
Bhatia said the purpose of an emergency fund was not to maximise returns but to ensure easy access to money when needed.
 
Investors could keep an amount equivalent to one or two months of expenses in a bank account. For the remaining amount, they could consider options like bank fixed deposits (FDs), liquid funds and overnight funds.
 
However, mutual fund investments carry risks and returns are not guaranteed. Investors should avoid parking emergency funds in equity funds.
 
Mistakes investors should avoid
 
Agrawal cautioned investors against taking excessive risks in an attempt to recover losses quickly during a market downturn.
 
Switching funds solely on the basis of six months of poor performance, taking excessive exposure to smallcap or sectoral funds, and selling investments in panic could prove detrimental.
 
According to Agrawal, investors with stable incomes and adequate savings need not discontinue their SIPs merely because markets are falling.
 
Bhatia, meanwhile, said those facing uncertainty over employment or income could temporarily reduce their investments and increase savings. SIP contributions could be raised again once their financial circumstances improve.
